title: Patti Harrison Had Dreams of a Tech Utopia. Silicon Valley Smashed Them
gist: Comedian Patti Harrison, interviewed by WIRED's Katie Drummond, argues that capitalism and monopolization corrupted the utopian promise of technology she believed in as a kid, citing addictive social-media algorithms, dual-use robotics deployed in Gaza, AI content-moderation failures, and a resulting consumer swing toward physical/analog and live experiences.

insights.claim: Harrison argues that capitalism systematically corrupts promising technology: once an industry finds 'the best way' to do something, a dominant player buys or captures that approach and then withdraws it, leaving consumers with degraded versions of what used to be good (she cites ad-free, non-algorithmic, chronological-feed social media as an example of a 'good' version that was later taken away).
insights.speaker: Patti Harrison
insights.so_what: Frames platform monopolization and enshittification as a recurring, structural pattern investors should expect to repeat with emerging tech categories (e.g., AI products), not a one-off social media problem.
insights.quote: once they see the best way we can have it, someone buys that way and then takes it away from everybody so that they can offer us shittier versions of the thing that used to be good.
insights.locator: But then there’s the disillusionment that comes with realizing that capitalism will sour everything

insights.claim: Harrison claims robotics companies (in the context of Boston Dynamics-style robot dogs) promised their technology would not be used in combat, yet such robots are now reportedly being used in Gaza, which she frames as evidence of a broken promise around dual-use military applications of consumer/industrial robotics.
insights.speaker: Patti Harrison
insights.so_what: A claim of civilian-to-military mission creep in robotics is a governance/ethics risk flag for investors in robotics and defense-adjacent hardware companies, regardless of whether it can be independently verified.
insights.quote: These companies, when they’re developing these robotics that have the potential to really hurt people, they promise these aren’t gonna be used in combat. We see them using these robot dogs in Gaza.
insights.locator: I don’t have a way to reconcile that at this point

themes.theme: Social media platform economics and creator dependency

insights.claim: Harrison asserts that social media platforms deliberately test features designed to maximize user addiction, and that the resulting revenue flows upward, funding what she calls 'bad people' while users individually blame themselves rather than the systemic incentive structure.
insights.speaker: Patti Harrison
insights.so_what: Supports the broader thesis that engagement-optimized platform design is an intentional, tested business practice rather than incidental, relevant to regulatory and ad-revenue risk assessments of social platforms.
insights.quote: they are testing these features to make sure that people become addicted.
insights.locator: All that time is wasted. Our lives are wasted

insights.claim: Harrison credits her acting career breakthrough (being discovered by Tim Robinson) directly to her social media presence, and describes feeling economically trapped by platform dependency, fearing that deleting her account would end her income.
insights.speaker: Patti Harrison
insights.so_what: Illustrates a structural dynamic in the creator economy: platforms capture creators' career/income leverage, making it economically costly for talent to exit even when they recognize the platform's harms.
insights.quote: I do personally have this sense of like, ‘Oh no, if I delete this, this will end my income.’ It’s really designed to make you feel that way, which is insidious
insights.locator: I think I read that Tim Robinson found you on Instagram

insights.claim: Harrison reports that Instagram's AI-driven content moderation flagged and removed a post as 'bullying and abuse' for a benign joke, while direct harassment and death-adjacent comments she reported against herself were ruled not in violation of community guidelines, illustrating inconsistent AI moderation enforcement.
insights.speaker: Patti Harrison
insights.so_what: A concrete, first-hand data point of AI content-moderation false positives/negatives at a major platform, relevant to trust & safety and regulatory scrutiny of automated moderation systems.
insights.quote: when they started using AI to comb through people’s posts, I had a lot flagged that were like, ‘This post was taken down for bullying and abuse.’
insights.locator: It’s amazing, the hypocrisy of the right wing

themes.theme: AI: environmental cost, adoption pace, and creative displacement

insights.claim: Harrison criticizes the pace of AI deployment as happening 'without any sort of vetting' for profit, and specifically names data centers as environmentally destructive, arguing that commercial incentives are pushing companies to expedite AI rollout faster than appropriate safeguards allow.
insights.speaker: Patti Harrison
insights.so_what: Reflects a public-sentiment data point (from a culturally influential figure) around AI infrastructure environmental backlash, a theme relevant to social license and ESG scrutiny of AI/data-center buildouts.
insights.quote: Data centers are destroying the environment. I think there are people out there who are trying to get them to stop and take the appropriate amount of time before this is implemented
insights.locator: I want to talk to you about AI. Do you use it?

insights.claim: Harrison deliberately avoids recording her live comedy shows into specials, partly to prevent her material from being absorbed/scraped by AI and partly because she believes jokes lose their effect out of context in short clips, treating live, unrecorded performance as a hedge against AI content replication.
insights.speaker: Patti Harrison
insights.so_what: Signals a behavioral response among creative professionals to AI training-data scraping risk: withholding recorded content and leaning into in-person/live formats as a defensive strategy.
insights.quote: If I’m online, it’s inevitable that AI will absorb it. I have had the most fun in my career doing live shows and being in a room with an audience
insights.locator: Are there things that scare you about it creatively and artistically?

insights.claim: Harrison predicts AI-hologram versions of deceased or absent performers (e.g., 'Come see George Carlin's AI') as a plausible future commercial offering, implying a coming market for AI-driven simulated live entertainment.
insights.speaker: Patti Harrison
insights.so_what: Flags AI-generated/hologram entertainment as an anticipated product category worth watching in live-events and IP-licensing markets.
insights.quote: unless we have AI hologram comedians that people come to see, which I’m sure has already been on the table. Like, ‘Come see George Carlin’s AI.’
insights.locator: I do think that as long as people will come and be in a space

insights.claim: Harrison observes a growing consumer pull toward analog and physical products (e.g., print magazines, in-person events) as a reaction against AI-generated content ('AI slop') and platforms, and frames it as a genuine, noticeable shift in her own content feed and audience behavior.
insights.speaker: Patti Harrison
insights.so_what: A qualitative signal of demand resurgence for physical/analog and live-event formats that could inform investment theses around print, live entertainment, and physical media as an AI-era counter-trend, though the speaker flags her own view may be algorithmically biased.
insights.quote: I do feel like I get a lot of content of people turning toward analog things across the board, and that is an exciting thing to me.
insights.locator: You’re pointing at something interesting that I think is true

insights.claim: Harrison notes that digital purchases (e.g., video games without physical discs) reduce packaging waste but strip buyers of true ownership, since platforms can revoke access to purchased digital content when they remove it from their marketplace, which she says drives consumer demand for owning physical goods.
insights.speaker: Patti Harrison
insights.so_what: Digital-ownership revocation risk is cited as a direct driver of a physical-goods preference trend, relevant to platforms' digital storefront policies and consumer trust in digital rights.
insights.quote: we’re learning that companies are like, ‘No, you actually don’t own that. You don’t actually own that the day we decide we don’t wanna keep it on our marketplace anymore.’
insights.locator: If we’re moving video games from being a physical purchase

insights.claim: Harrison states that what gives her hope is a rise in class consciousness and growing public interest in socialism, which she links to people recognizing they are getting 'the worst version of everything' under the current capitalist system.
insights.speaker: Patti Harrison
insights.so_what: A data point on shifting political-economic sentiment among culturally influential younger/creative-class figures, relevant to reading consumer and labor-market attitudes toward corporate power.
insights.quote: I think what gives me hope is the rise in class consciousness and the rising interest in socialism.
